items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow the programmer's code fixes the steps in advance, in an agent the model decides the next step as it goes. Both can call a model (a), and handling requests one at a time or many at once (c) has nothing to do with it; reversing the roles (d) is the opposite of the definition.

Only in d does the model choose the tools, their order and when to stop, which is what makes it an agent. In a, b and c the code fixes the path; calling a model once or several times inside a fixed path does not change who owns the control flow.

When the next step depends on what comes back and no fixed sequence covers the cases, the model has to choose the steps, so an agent is worth its extra model calls. A fixed workflow cannot cover this path (c), and neither design is always cheaper (b) or always more reliable (d); the choice follows whether the steps are known in advance.

When the steps are known and the same every time, a fixed workflow gives predictable cost, is easier to test, and does not pay for model decisions. An agent is not automatically more reliable (a) or cheaper (b), since every decision costs a model call, and a workflow can call tools just as well (d).
The agent makes 3 tool-request calls plus 1 final-answer call = 4 calls per question; the workflow makes 2. The difference is 4 - 2 = 2 per question, and 2 x 50 = 100.

The code decides when to retry and when to stop, and the model only writes text at each step, so the code still owns the control flow: it is a workflow with a loop in it. A loop (a) or several model calls (c) does not make an agent; the question is who decides the next step. A retry (d) does not hand the control to the model.
